nodes.label: Forest Stakeholders
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Four main stakeholders in forest management: (1) local people dependent on forest produce for livelihood (firewood, timber, bamboo, food, fodder, medicines), (2) Forest Department of the Government (owns land, controls resources), (3) industrialists using forest produce (tendu leaves for bidis, paper mills -- not dependent on any single forest area), (4) wildlife and nature conservation enthusiasts. Each group has different interests that must be balanced.

nodes.label: DNA as Genetic Material
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Griffith's experiment (1928) with Streptococcus pneumoniae showed 'transforming principle' - heat-killed S strain + live R strain killed mice. Avery, MacLeod, McCarty (1933-44) proved the transforming principle was DNA (not protein or RNA). Hershey-Chase experiment (1952) with bacteriophages using radioactive phosphorus (P-32 for DNA) and sulfur (S-35 for protein) conclusively proved DNA is genetic material. DNA contains phosphorus but not sulfur; protein contains sulfur but not phosphorus.

nodes.label: RNA World Hypothesis
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: RNA was the first genetic material. Evidence suggests essential life processes (metabolism, translation, splicing) evolved around RNA. RNA can act as both genetic material AND catalyst (ribozymes). However, RNA is reactive and unstable due to 2'-OH group, making it labile and degradable. DNA evolved from RNA with chemical modifications (deoxyribose, thymine instead of uracil) making it more stable. DNA's double-stranded complementary structure enables repair mechanisms. Central Dogma: DNA -> RNA -> Protein (proposed by Crick).

nodes.label: Transcription
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Copying of genetic information from one DNA strand into RNA. Template strand has 3'->5' polarity; coding strand has 5'->3' polarity (same sequence as RNA except T for U). Transcription unit has three parts: Promoter (5' upstream, RNA polymerase binding), Structural gene, Terminator (3' downstream). In bacteria: single RNA polymerase for all RNA types; uses sigma factor for initiation, rho factor for termination. Transcription and translation coupled in bacteria. In eukaryotes: three RNA polymerases (I for rRNA, II for mRNA/hnRNA, III for tRNA/5S rRNA/snRNA).

nodes.label: RNA Processing in Eukaryotes
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Primary transcript (hnRNA) in eukaryotes contains both exons (coding sequences) and introns (intervening non-coding sequences). Split gene arrangement is an ancient feature. Processing involves: splicing (removal of introns, joining of exons), capping (methyl guanosine triphosphate added at 5' end), and tailing/polyadenylation (200-300 adenylate residues at 3' end). Fully processed hnRNA becomes mRNA, which is then transported from nucleus to cytoplasm for translation. Transcription and translation are NOT coupled in eukaryotes.

nodes.label: Genetic Code
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Triplet code proposed by George Gamow (physicist): 4^3 = 64 codons from 4 bases. Deciphered by Har Gobind Khorana (chemical synthesis of RNA) and Marshall Nirenberg (cell-free protein synthesis). Properties: (1) triplet codons, (2) degenerate (most amino acids coded by more than one codon), (3) non-overlapping and comma-less (read contiguously), (4) nearly universal (bacteria to humans), (5) AUG is start codon (codes for methionine) and initiator, (6) UAA, UAG, UGA are stop codons. 61 codons for amino acids + 3 stop codons = 64 total.

nodes.label: Translation (Protein Synthesis)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Polymerisation of amino acids to form polypeptide, directed by mRNA sequence. tRNA is the adapter molecule with anticodon loop (reads code) and amino acid acceptor end. Ribosomes are the cellular factory (structural rRNAs + ~80 proteins). Translation starts at AUG with initiator tRNA, elongates as ribosome moves codon by codon adding amino acids via peptide bonds, and terminates at stop codon (UAA/UAG/UGA) when release factor binds. 23S rRNA acts as ribozyme catalysing peptide bond formation in bacteria.

nodes.label: Lac Operon
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Model of gene regulation in E. coli, elucidated by Jacob and Monod. Contains: regulatory gene (i gene, codes for repressor), and three structural genes - z (beta-galactosidase, hydrolyses lactose), y (permease, allows lactose entry), a (transacetylase). In absence of lactose: repressor binds operator, blocks RNA polymerase, genes not transcribed. In presence of lactose (inducer): lactose/allolactose inactivates repressor, RNA polymerase transcribes structural genes. Example of negative regulation. Glucose and galactose cannot act as inducers.

nodes.label: Point Mutation and Frameshift Mutation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Point mutation: change of a single base pair in DNA. Classic example: sickle-cell anaemia (beta-globin gene GAG->GUG, glutamate->valine). Frameshift mutation: insertion or deletion of one or two bases changes the reading frame from that point onward, altering all subsequent codons. Insertion/deletion of three bases (or multiples) adds/removes whole codons without disrupting the reading frame. Mutations can be caused by mutagens including UV radiation and chemicals.

nodes.label: Central Dogma of Molecular Biology
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Proposed by Francis Crick: genetic information flows from DNA to RNA to Protein. DNA replicates itself (replication). DNA is transcribed to mRNA (transcription). mRNA is translated to protein (translation). In some viruses (retroviruses), reverse flow occurs from RNA to DNA (reverse transcription). The dogma established the informational hierarchy in biology: DNA stores information, RNA transmits it, and proteins execute cellular functions.

nodes.label: Key Experiments Proving DNA as Genetic Material
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Three landmark experiments: (1) Griffith (1928) - transformation experiment with S. pneumoniae showing heat-killed S strain transforms live R strain. (2) Avery, MacLeod, McCarty (1933-44) - proved transforming principle is DNA by showing DNase (not protease or RNase) inhibits transformation. (3) Hershey and Chase (1952) - used radioactive P-32 (labels DNA) and S-35 (labels protein) in bacteriophages to prove only DNA enters bacteria during infection. These experiments definitively established DNA as the hereditary material.

nodes.label: Microbes in Household Products
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Lactobacillus and other lactic acid bacteria (LAB) convert milk to curd by producing acids that coagulate and partially digest milk proteins. Curd has increased vitamin B12. LAB in stomach check disease-causing microbes. Dosa, idli dough fermented by bacteria (CO2 puffs dough). Bread dough fermented by baker's yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Swiss cheese has large holes due to CO2 by Propionibacterium sharmanii. Roquefort cheese ripened by specific fungi for flavour.

nodes.label: Fermented Beverages
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Yeasts (Saccharomyces cerevisiae/brewer's yeast) used since ancient times to produce wine, beer, whisky, brandy, rum by fermenting malted cereals and fruit juices to produce ethanol. Wine and beer produced without distillation; whisky, brandy, rum produced by distillation of fermented broth. Toddy is a traditional south Indian drink made by fermenting palm sap. Industrial scale production uses large vessels called fermentors.

nodes.label: Antibiotics
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Chemical substances produced by microbes that kill or retard growth of disease-causing microbes. Penicillin was first antibiotic, discovered by Alexander Fleming from mould Penicillium notatum growing on Staphylococci culture plate. Full potential established by Ernest Chain and Howard Florey. Nobel Prize 1945 to Fleming, Chain, Florey. Used extensively on American soldiers in WWII. Antibiotics treat plague, whooping cough (kali khansi), diphtheria (gal ghotu), leprosy (kusht rog).

nodes.label: Industrial Chemicals, Enzymes and Bioactive Molecules
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Acid producers: Aspergillus niger (citric acid), Acetobacter aceti (acetic acid), Clostridium butylicum (butyric acid), Lactobacillus (lactic acid). Saccharomyces cerevisiae produces ethanol commercially. Enzymes: lipases (detergent formulations for oily stains), pectinases and proteases (clarify bottled fruit juices). Streptokinase from Streptococcus (clot buster for myocardial infarction). Cyclosporin A from Trichoderma polysporum (immunosuppressant in organ transplants). Statins from Monascus purpureus (yeast) - blood cholesterol lowering by competitively inhibiting cholesterol synthesis enzyme.

nodes.label: Biocontrol Agents
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Use of biological methods to control plant diseases and pests instead of toxic chemicals. Ladybird beetles control aphids; dragonflies control mosquitoes. Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt): dried spores sprayed on plants, eaten by insect larvae; toxin released in gut kills larvae but other insects unharmed. Bt toxin genes introduced into plants via genetic engineering (Bt-cotton). Trichoderma: free-living fungi in root ecosystems, effective biocontrol agents of plant pathogens. Baculoviruses (genus Nucleopolyhedrovirus): species-specific insecticidal agents, no negative impact on plants/mammals/birds/fish/non-target insects. Used in IPM.

nodes.label: Biofertilisers
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Organisms that enrich nutrient quality of soil. Main sources: bacteria, fungi, cyanobacteria. Rhizobium: symbiotic nitrogen fixation in root nodules of leguminous plants. Azospirillum and Azotobacter: free-living soil bacteria that fix atmospheric nitrogen. Mycorrhiza (e.g., Glomus): fungal symbiont absorbs phosphorus from soil and passes to plant; provides resistance to root-borne pathogens, tolerance to salinity and drought, overall increase in plant growth. Cyanobacteria (Anabaena, Nostoc, Oscillatoria): autotrophic, fix nitrogen, important biofertiliser in paddy fields, add organic matter to soil.

nodes.label: Penicillin Discovery
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: First antibiotic discovered by Alexander Fleming - a chance discovery. While working on Staphylococci bacteria, Fleming observed a mould (Penicillium notatum) growing in unwashed culture plate around which Staphylococci could not grow. Named the chemical Penicillin. Full potential as effective antibiotic established later by Ernest Chain and Howard Florey. Fleming, Chain, Florey won Nobel Prize in 1945. Extensively used to treat wounded American soldiers in World War II.

nodes.label: Streptokinase
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Produced by bacterium Streptococcus and modified by genetic engineering. Used as a 'clot buster' for removing blood clots from vessels of patients who have had myocardial infarction (heart attack). Important example of industrial enzyme with medical application.

nodes.label: Cyclosporin A
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Bioactive molecule produced by the fungus Trichoderma polysporum. Used as an immunosuppressive agent in organ-transplant patients to prevent rejection. Important pharmaceutical product derived from microbes.

nodes.label: Statins
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Produced by yeast Monascus purpureus. Commercialised as blood-cholesterol lowering agents. Mechanism: competitively inhibits the enzyme responsible for synthesis of cholesterol. Important pharmaceutical product from microbial source.

nodes.label: Bacteria
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Single-celled microorganisms found in virtually every environment on Earth. Some are beneficial (Lactobacillus for curd, Rhizobium for nitrogen fixation), while others cause diseases like tuberculosis, typhoid, and cholera. They are among the hardiest organisms, surviving extreme conditions.

nodes.label: Virus
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Microscopic agents that reproduce only inside the cells of a host organism (bacterium, plant, or animal). Unlike bacteria, they lack cellular structure. They cause diseases like common cold, influenza, polio, chicken pox, dengue, and AIDS. Antibiotics are ineffective against viral infections.

nodes.label: Nitrogen Cycle
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The biogeochemical cycle maintaining the constant percentage of nitrogen (78%) in the atmosphere. Nitrogen is fixed by bacteria and lightning, absorbed by plants through roots, used for protein synthesis, consumed by animals, and returned to soil by decomposers. Denitrifying bacteria release nitrogen gas back to the atmosphere.

nodes.label: Alexander Fleming
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: British scientist who in 1929 discovered penicillin when he observed that the mould Penicillium prevented the growth of bacteria in his culture plates. This accidental discovery revolutionised medicine and led to the development of antibiotics that have saved millions of lives.

nodes.label: Synthetic Fibres
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Man-made fibres produced by chemical processing of petrochemicals. They are durable, less expensive, readily available, easy to maintain, dry quickly, and can be woven like natural fibres. However, they melt on heating and should not be worn near fire. Major types include rayon, nylon, polyester, and acrylic.

nodes.label: Rayon
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Also called artificial silk, rayon is obtained by chemical treatment of wood pulp (cellulose). Though derived from a natural source, it is a man-made fibre. Cheaper than silk, it can be woven and dyed in various colours. Mixed with cotton for bed sheets and with wool for carpets.

nodes.label: Nylon
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The first fully synthetic fibre, prepared from coal, water, and air in 1931 without any natural raw material. Strong, elastic, light, lustrous, and easy to wash. A nylon thread is stronger than a steel wire. Used for stockings, ropes, parachutes, tents, toothbrushes, and car seat belts.

nodes.label: Polyester
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A synthetic fibre made of repeating units of esters (chemicals giving fruits their smell). Fabric does not wrinkle easily, remains crisp, and is easy to wash. Terylene is a popular polyester. PET (polyethylene terephthalate) is used for bottles, utensils, films, and wires.

nodes.label: Acrylic
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A synthetic fibre used as a cheaper alternative to natural wool for making sweaters, shawls, and blankets. Available in a variety of colours and more durable than natural wool, making it popular despite being artificially produced.

nodes.label: Petrochemicals
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Raw materials of petroleum origin used for manufacturing all synthetic fibres and many plastics. These include chemicals derived from the refining of petroleum and natural gas, forming the basis of the modern synthetic materials industry.

nodes.label: PCRA
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The Petroleum Conservation Research Association, an Indian body that advises people on saving petrol and diesel. Tips include driving at constant moderate speed, switching off engines at traffic lights, ensuring correct tyre pressure, and regular vehicle maintenance.

nodes.label: National Park
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Areas reserved for wildlife where animals can freely use habitats and natural resources. These are large and diverse enough to protect whole ecosystems. Satpura National Park is the first Reserve Forest of India. There are more than one hundred National Parks in India. Human activities are strictly prohibited.

nodes.label: Mixture
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A combination of two or more pure substances where each retains its own properties. Components can be separated by physical methods. Most substances in nature exist as mixtures. Examples include air, sea water, milk, and soil. Components are present in variable ratios.

nodes.label: Homogeneous Mixture (Solution)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A mixture with uniform composition throughout where individual components cannot be distinguished. Also called a solution. Examples include salt in water, sugar in water, and air. The solute particles are extremely small (less than 1 nm) and cannot scatter light.

nodes.label: Heterogeneous Mixture
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A mixture without uniform composition where individual components can be distinguished. Examples include a mixture of salt and iron filings, oil and water, and soil. Components can often be separated by simple physical methods like handpicking or filtration.

nodes.label: Solution
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A homogeneous mixture of two or more substances consisting of a solute (dissolved substance) and a solvent (dissolving medium). Can be solid, liquid, or gas. Alloys like brass (copper + zinc) are solid solutions. Concentration expressed as mass percentage.

nodes.label: Colloid
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A heterogeneous mixture where particles are between 1 nm and 100 nm in size, too small to be seen individually but large enough to scatter light (Tyndall effect). Examples include milk, fog, butter, blood, and ink. Cannot be separated by filtration but can by centrifugation.

nodes.label: Suspension
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A heterogeneous mixture with particles larger than 100 nm that are visible to the naked eye and scatter light. Particles settle down over time. Examples include muddy water, chalk in water, and smoke. Can be separated by filtration.

nodes.label: Separation Techniques
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Physical methods for separating components of mixtures. Include evaporation, distillation, fractional distillation, chromatography, crystallisation, centrifugation, and separating funnel. Choice depends on the physical and chemical properties of the components.

nodes.label: Chromatography
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A technique for separating components of a mixture based on their different rates of movement through a medium. Used in separating colours in a dye, pigments from natural colours, and drugs from blood. The word means colour writing.

nodes.label: Neutron
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: An electrically neutral subatomic particle found in the nucleus, discovered by James Chadwick in 1932. Mass is approximately equal to that of a proton. The number of neutrons can vary among atoms of the same element, creating isotopes.

nodes.label: Infectious Diseases
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Diseases caused by microorganisms (pathogens) that can spread from one person to another through air, water, food, vectors, or physical contact. Also called communicable diseases. Examples: common cold, TB, cholera, malaria, AIDS, dengue. Treatment depends on the type of pathogen.

nodes.label: Non-infectious Diseases
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Diseases that cannot spread from person to person. Caused by internal factors like genetic abnormalities, nutritional deficiencies, hormonal imbalances, or lifestyle choices. Examples: diabetes, cancer, heart disease, high blood pressure, allergies.

nodes.label: Infectious Agents
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Microorganisms that cause diseases, categorised as viruses (cold, flu, AIDS, dengue), bacteria (TB, cholera, typhoid, anthrax), fungi (skin infections), protozoans (malaria, kala-azar), and worms (elephantiasis, intestinal infections). Category determines treatment approach.

nodes.label: Antibiotics in Treatment
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Drugs that block biochemical pathways important for bacteria, such as cell-wall synthesis (penicillin). Effective against many bacterial species but completely ineffective against viruses because viruses do not use these pathways. Overuse leads to antibiotic resistance.

nodes.label: Means of Disease Spread
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Infectious diseases spread through: air (cold, TB, pneumonia via droplets), water (cholera via contaminated water), sexual contact (syphilis, AIDS), and vectors like mosquitoes (malaria via Anopheles, dengue via Aedes). Crowded living conditions increase airborne disease transmission.

nodes.label: Tuberculosis (TB)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A chronic infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis bacteria, primarily affecting the lungs. Spreads through air via droplets from coughing and sneezing. Treatable with antibiotics over several months. One of the most significant infectious diseases globally.

nodes.label: Organ-Specific Disease Manifestation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Different microbes target different organs based on their entry point and tissue preference. TB bacteria entering through the nose affect lungs, HIV attacks the immune system, Japanese encephalitis virus affects the brain. Organ damage determines disease symptoms and severity.

nodes.label: Vectors of Disease
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Animals that carry infecting agents from sick to healthy persons without being affected themselves. Mosquitoes are the commonest vectors: female Anopheles transmits malaria (Plasmodium), female Aedes transmits dengue. Vector control (eliminating breeding sites) is key to prevention.
